Campaign agent-harnesses · dsh @ 47f9438 · nothing on this page is hidden

Harness Dissection

Build a transferable model of agent harnesses as a category by dissecting DeepSeek Harness — then test whether that model explains a harness it was never derived from.

specimen deepseek-harness pinned 47f9438 · 2026-08-13 packages 49, all covered threads 15 — 12 open, 3 need evidence transfer test Claude Code transcripts completion none — surprise budget
§ 1

The loop everything else is filed under

A language model is a function from text to text. It cannot read a file, run a command, or remember anything. A harness is the program wrapped around it that supplies all three. Everything else — compaction, permissions, plugins, sandboxing, delegation — is a refinement of one of these five steps, which is why §4 files each of the fifteen threads under the step it explains.

Three claims the whole plan rests on

You can't read what you can't name

Writing a harness first supplies the vocabulary that makes a real one legible. Reading agent-loop cold teaches nothing; reading it after writing a loop teaches everything.

The wire beats the source

Prompt assembly is scattered across dozens of files. The bytes sent to the API are single, literal ground truth. When a reading and a capture disagree, the capture wins.

A vocabulary must transfer

Concepts that only explain their own specimen are worthless. The study succeeds if ideas derived from dsh explain Claude Code — and fails if they don't.

§ 2

The map · what blocks what

0 → 1 → 2.0 is a strict chain; everything after it fans out. The fifteen threads have no order among themselves — but two things downstream are gated, and one of them is gated on a finding, not a phase. The five columns are the five steps of the loop above; click one to jump to its band.

§ 3

The board · what you can start now

The same five phases as the map, sorted by what is blocking each card rather than by phase number. The left lane needs nothing but a terminal; the right lane must stay last or the study invalidates itself.

Task 0.1
Pin the checkout

Clone, detach at 47f9438, install frozen, build. Then discover and record the base-URL override and the non-interactive run command.

# pin the specimen
git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git \
  ../deepseek-harness
git -C ../deepseek-harness checkout 47f943859bef60e4160492346772ded9b24f765a

# build it
cd ../deepseek-harness && corepack enable
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build

# find the base-URL override — this is what lets you capture later
rg -n 'baseURL|baseUrl|base_url|BASE_URL' packages/llm/ apps/ --type ts

produces LLM_BASE_URL_ENV · DSH_CMD

Task 0.2
Build the capture proxy

~70 lines of dependency-free Node. Tees SSE to disk without buffering the client's view, and redacts authorization, x-api-key, api-key, cookie before any write.

The one check you must not skip
node tools/capture-proxy/leak-check.mjs captures/*.jsonl
# must print: clean: N captures, no credential found

A leaked key in a capture is the single unrecoverable mistake in this study. The check runs two ways, because they fail differently: structurally, every sensitive header must read &lt;redacted&gt;, which catches a redaction bug even for a credential format nobody anticipated; and by shape, key-like strings are hunted anywhere in the file, including bodies, where a model may have echoed a secret the proxy never saw as a header. If it reports a leak, stop, fix redact(), and treat the key as burned — rotate it rather than deleting the file, because it existed on disk in that state.

Deliverables: .gitignore, tools/capture-proxy/server.mjs, and notes/00-orientation.md holding the pinned SHA, the package map, and the two discovered values every later task consumes by name.

Phase 1 · the control
Write a harness from scratch

~45 lines against the DeepSeek API: a message list, two tools, a loop, a step cap. The only harness whose every byte you can account for — and therefore the reference against which dsh's captures are read.

messages = [system, user]
for step in 1..10:
    msg = POST /chat/completions {model, messages, tools}
    messages.push(msg)
    if not msg.tool_calls: print(msg.content); break
    for call in msg.tool_calls:
        result = impls[call.name](call.args)
        messages.push({role:'tool', tool_call_id,
          content: result.slice(0,4000)})

Then break it deliberately:

  • Blow the truncation — read package-lock.json and list the dependencies.
  • Blow the step cap — twelve sorting algorithms, each run and compared.
  • Expose the missing permission layer — delete every .tmp under /tmp. The alarm you feel is packages/guard's entire reason to exist.

Deliverables: experiments/minimal-harness/harness.mjs, a capture of your own harness through the proxy, and notes/01-what-my-harness-lacks.md — the table that becomes §4 and §5. First real CONTEXT.md terms land here: loop, turn, step, tool call, tool result, context window.

Task 2.0 · observation only
Baseline capture of dsh

Capture dsh on the canonical task, then write notes/02-baseline-behavior.md recording only what was observable: round-trip count, tool order, when approval was requested, what displayed between steps, whether it verified its own work.

rg -n 'packages/' notes/02-baseline-behavior.md
# must print nothing

That note is the control Thread B must later reconcile against, line by line. It only works if it was written before you read any source.

Then diff your toy against the specimen: same task, two harnesses, two captures. Every difference is a thread to pull.

Phase 3
One tool, two harnesses

The same trivial tool built twice — as a dsh plugin and as an MCP server for Claude Code. The diff between the two integrations is the finding.

Two things must be true, per harness: the tool was offered, and the model called it. Proving only the first is the classic false pass — it shows registration worked while the loop never closed around it.

# offered (dsh, from the capture)
jq -r 'select(.dir=="request") | .body.tools[]? | .function.name' \
  captures/session-plugin.jsonl | sort -u | rg hello_study

# called (either harness — grep the marker)
rg -c 'STUDY-MARKER-7f3a' captures/session-plugin.jsonl

Why this is the category exam: what both harnesses demand of a tool is essential to the category. What only one demands is incidental to its implementation. That intersection is the real model of “a tool” — and MCP versus a Cordis plugin is itself an answer to Thread E's question about where an extension boundary belongs.

blocked by Thread D only — it does not wait for the other fourteen

Phase 4
Transfer test

Commit predictions before opening the Claude Code transcripts already on disk, then score them. Sort every glossary term into universal, dsh-specific, or missing.

Predict first, and commit the prediction. From the dsh-derived model alone, write down which tools you expect, how results appear serialized, what stop reasons exist, how permissions are gated. A prediction made after looking tests nothing — so it goes in a commit before the first jq runs.

Three buckets, and two of them are the output:

  • Universal — explains both harnesses. Stays canonical in CONTEXT.md.
  • dsh-specific — an implementation detail you mistook for a category concept.
  • Missing — Claude Code does something your vocabulary can't name. thinking blocks, hooks, and sidechains are the likely candidates.

Buckets two and three are what the study actually produced. Bucket one is just what survived.

blocked by all of Phase 2 · see §6 for what transcripts can and can't show

Step 1 · Assemble What goes into the request, and what gets left out? 3 threads · 9 packages
APrompt & presentation

What actually belongs in a system prompt, and how much behaviour is bought with prose rather than code?

FROM two tools in an array literal · one hard-coded system prompt string

core/system-promptagent-tool-presentationpresetneeds a dsh capture
jq -r 'select(.dir=="request") | .body.messages[]
  | select(.role=="system") | .content' \
  captures/session-dsh-canonical.jsonl | head -1

Answer with a number. What fraction of behavioural instruction lives in tool descriptions versus the system prompt? That ratio is a category-level property you can carry to any harness.

Take a distinctive six-word phrase from the capture and rg for it. If it isn't found literally, the prompt is assembled from fragments — record which, and where.

→ worklog

CContext & compaction

What should be dropped when the context fills, and is the decision positional, semantic, or size-based?

FROM .slice(0, 4000) on every tool result

compaction/*contextspillcore/sessionneeds a dsh capture
jq -r 'select(.dir=="request")
  | "\(.id)\t\(.body.messages|length)\t\(.body.messages|tostring|length)"' \
  captures/session-dsh-long.jsonl

A monotonic rise followed by a drop in message count is a compaction event. The canonical task is too short to trigger one — run the twelve-algorithm task instead.

The densest engineering in the repo: compaction is a top-level package with a dedicated compaction-tool-result-pruner, and spill sits alongside it. Direct answer to your toy's worst shortcut.

MInputs & code intelligence

What does a harness feed the model besides text and tool results?

FROM the package census — the toy never raised this one

attachmentlsp

attachment: how are images and files injected — re-sent every turn, or referenced? That has a direct cost consequence; connect it to Thread C.

lsp: the harness runs a language server and hands the model its output. Determine whether that arrives as a tool the model calls, or as context injected without being asked. Those are very different designs — decide which is better, and why dsh chose as it did.

→ worklog

Step 2 · Call What sits between the harness and any model provider? 1 thread · 6 packages
LProvider abstraction

What does it take to be model-agnostic, and where does the abstraction leak?

FROM hard-coding one provider's wire format

llm/*llm-deepseekllm-pi-aillm-retrycredentialsidentity

Read the shared llm interface, then both implementations behind it. What sits in the interface that only one provider actually needs? That is where the abstraction leaks.

Then llm-retry: which failures are retried, with what backoff, and is a retried call visible to the loop or hidden beneath it? A hidden retry changes what “one step” means.

The category question: can a harness be genuinely model-agnostic, given that prompt engineering, tool-call formats, and thinking blocks all differ per model?

→ worklog

Steps 3–4 · Parse · Execute What the model asked for — and what is allowed to happen as a result. 4 threads · 18 packages
DTools & permission

What must a harness be told about a tool, and where does the permission boundary sit?

FROM running every tool unchecked, including rm · two tools in an array literal

core/toolsfsguardwebgates Phase 3
rg -n 'approve|permission|confirm|allow|deny' packages/guard --type ts

Trace the file-edit tool through six layers, each cited path:line: schema → registration → presentation → dispatch → permission → result serialization.

Then answer: is approval per-call, per-tool, per-session, or path-scoped — and what's the default posture? Output is a harness-neutral checklist, “what a new tool must provide,” which Phase 3 consumes directly.

→ worklog · D-tools-and-permission.md

FDelegation & sub-agents

When does a harness spawn another harness, and what does the child inherit?

FROM one loop, one context, no fan-out

subagentplangoaljobsscheduleCC comparison
rg -n 'fork|spawn|child|sub.?agent|delegate' \
  packages/subagent packages/jobs --type ts

The design question is what a child inherits — tools? history? permissions? — and how its result re-enters the parent's context.

One of the sharpest comparison surfaces in the study. Claude Code has the same feature: sub-agent invocations appear in transcripts as Task/Agent tool calls, and isSidechain marks the child sessions.

→ worklog

GExecution & sandboxing

Where does model-authored code actually run, and what contains it?

FROM bare execSync on the host

sandboxe2bcode-runtimeshellsubprocessterminal
rg -n 'unsafe|escape|host|local|bypass' packages/sandbox --type ts

Six packages here against your toy's bare execSync — that alone says the answer isn't obvious. Distinguish the layers: is code-runtime the abstraction, sandbox the local implementation, e2b a remote provider?

Then find the escape hatch — is there a path where code runs unsandboxed, and what gates it? Map the isolation strategies (none / subprocess / container / remote VM) and what each costs in latency and fidelity.

→ worklog

OAgent self-management

What tools does a harness give the model for managing its own process, rather than the user's task?

FROM the model being unable to track its own plan

todoskillworkflowCC comparison

A category of tool your toy has no concept of: the model tracking its own plan, loading its own instructions, running predefined procedures. Every one has a direct Claude Code analogue, making this the densest comparison surface in the study.

  • todo — is the list context (re-sent every turn, costing tokens) or external state (stored, referenced)? That choice is the whole design question.
  • skill — does the model request one by name, or does the harness inject it on a match?
  • workflow — what distinguishes it from a plan (Thread F) and from a skill? If the code doesn't make that clear, the ambiguity is the finding.

→ worklog

Step 5 & the repeat · Control What makes it go round again — and what survives when it stops. 2 threads · 8 packages
BThe agent loop

What legitimately terminates a loop? Your toy just used a hard step cap of ten.

FROM hard-coded MAX_STEPS = 10

core/agent-loopcore/agentagent-default-modelneeds note 2.0
rg -n 'break|return|maxSteps|maxTurns|stop|finish' \
  packages/core/agent-loop --type ts
pnpm vitest run packages/core/agent-loop --reporter=verbose

Mark the line where each of the five phases happens, then record every termination condition in precedence order — no tool calls emitted, step cap, token budget, user interrupt.

The tests are executable spec: an invariant you wouldn't have predicted marks a gap in your model. Then reconcile every observation in notes/02-baseline-behavior.md against a specific line, or list it as open — which is why this one waits for Task 2.0.

→ worklog · B-agent-loop.md

IPersistence & resumption

What must be saved for a harness to resume a conversation it isn't currently holding in memory?

FROM losing everything on exit

sessionsession-querysettingsstorageworkspaceCC comparison
rg -n 'persist|save|write|serialize' packages/session --type ts

F=$(find ~/.claude/projects -name '*.jsonl' | head -1)
jq -r '.type' "$F" | sort | uniq -c

Your toy loses everything on exit. This is the thread with the richest comparison data, because Claude Code's own answer is sitting on your disk in ~3,800 files.

Then determine what session-query is for: is history searchable, and does the model get to search it, or only the user? That distinction is a real design fork.

→ worklog

Outside the loop · Around The frame the loop sits in — none of these is a step, and that is the point. 5 threads · 20 packages
EPlugin architecture

Where should a harness's extension boundary sit, and what does “everything is a plugin” make hard?

FROM no plugins, no extension points

core/scopebootextensionsbundle
cat packages/core/README.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md packages/AGENTS.md
rg -n 'ctx\.(plugin|on|set|inject)' packages/core --type ts

Learn Cordis first or this thread fails. It's dependency injection plus an event bus — nothing calls anything directly, so grep-based tracing finds nothing and the codebase reads as indirection with no call graph. There's a paper behind it: A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability.

The repo's own AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are written to orient agents working in it, which makes them the best human onboarding docs too — usually fresher than docs/.

→ worklog

HInterop · MCP & ACP

When a harness standardises its extension boundary, what does it give up?

FROM no plugins, no extension points

mcpacpapisdkCC comparison
cat packages/acp/README.md   # Agent Client Protocol — what connects to what?

Thread E covers the native extension boundary. This covers the standard one — and both harnesses under study speak MCP, making it the one integration surface you can compare directly.

The question that matters: which capabilities can a native plugin express that an MCP server cannot? That gap is precisely why native plugin systems still exist alongside MCP.

→ worklog

JObservability & cost

How does a harness let someone outside the loop observe it — or interrupt it?

FROM no way to observe or interrupt it

hooksfeedbackruntime-diagnosticstoken-meterCC comparison
rg -n 'hook|before|after|intercept' packages/hooks --type ts

Map the hook points: which loop phases can be intercepted, and can a hook block an action or only observe it? In Claude Code the answer is visible — preventedContinuation on system records proves hooks there can block.

token-meter connects straight back to Thread C: does the harness count tokens before sending (budgeting) or after (accounting)? That determines whether compaction can be predictive.

→ worklog · J-observability-and-cost.md

KThe host boundary

Where does the harness end and the user interface begin? Could you drive it with no UI at all?

FROM printing to stdout

hostclientinteractionapps/

Your toy printed to stdout. dsh serves a web UI on 127.0.0.1:3080, so it has drawn a boundary somewhere — and where that line sits determines whether the harness can be embedded, scripted, or driven headlessly.

Determine the transport between core and UI (HTTP, WebSocket, JSON-RPC, in-process?), and whether streaming reaches the UI as the raw model stream or as re-emitted domain events. Then answer the real question: what is the minimum surface a headless embedder needs?

→ worklog

NCross-language embedding

Can a TypeScript harness be driven from Python, and what does that boundary force it to make explicit?

FROM the package census — the toy never raised this one

python/native/sdkexamples

An RPC boundary forces the cleanest possible statement of what a harness is, because everything crossing it must be serialisable. BENCHMARK.md points at a Python SDK and a jsonrpc-agent variant.

Read the SDK's surface — that operation list is dsh's own answer to “what is the harness API?” Then compare it to your toy's function signatures: what did dsh have to make explicit that you left implicit?

§ 6

What the transfer test can and can't see

Claude Code here runs on a subscription, so it's studied through the ~3,800 session transcripts already on disk rather than through wire capture. Know these limits before predicting against it.

QuestionIn transcripts?Where it comes from
Which tools exist and get calledyestool_use blocks
How the loop terminatesyesstopReason
How permissions are gatedyespermission-mode
Whether hooks can blockyespreventedContinuation
Whether sub-agents fork contextyesisSidechain
Whether the model reasons before actingyesthinking blocks
What the system prompt saysnonot stored locally
What the tool schemas declarenonot stored locally

So Phase 4 tests the model of the loop, tools, and permissions — and stays silent on prompt assembly. That gap is a known cost of having no Anthropic API key, not an oversight.

§ 7

Standing orders

Six rules that hold in every phase and every thread. Read them once; they are assumed everywhere above.

The canonical task

Used verbatim for every harness so captures stay comparable — your toy, dsh, and Claude Code all get the same prompt: "Create a file called fizzbuzz.js that prints FizzBuzz for 1..20, then run it with node and show me the output." It forces read, write, and execute in one run.

The surprise budget

There is no completion criterion. Abandon a thread after two consecutive findings that don't surprise you, and file it as a needs-triage issue. A dry thread is a result, not a failure.

The wire wins

When your reading of the source and the captured bytes disagree, the reading is wrong. Fix the note, not the capture.

Never commit captures

captures/ is gitignored and the proxy redacts auth headers before writing. A leaked key in a capture is the one unrecoverable mistake here.

Analyse, don't dump

dsh's prompt ships in a public MIT repo and can be quoted freely. Claude Code transcripts are personal working history — cite structure, counts, and tool names only. This repo is public.

Glossary as you go

When a thread sharpens a term, it lands in CONTEXT.md that session — never batched to the end. Terms get re-sorted in Phase 4, and being wrong early is data.
